matthew.name: Matthew
matthew.tag: Jesus as the promised Messiah and King, the new Moses
facts: Matthew (Levi), the tax collector and one of the Twelve. The book itself does not name its author. Papias (about AD 110–130, quoted by Eusebius) says Matthew compiled the sayings of Jesus in the Hebrew style, and later writers tied that to this Gospel.
Most scholars say about AD 70–90, after Mark. Some argue for an earlier date. It was well known by about AD 110.
Often placed in Syria, perhaps Antioch. This is a guess.
Jewish-Christian readers who knew the Old Testament well. It quotes or echoes it constantly.
An ancient Greek biography, arranged by teaching and story.
Opens with the family tree of Jesus (1:1). Ends with “I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (28:20).
matthew.purpose: Matthew shows that Jesus is the Messiah the Scriptures promised: son of Abraham, son of David, and the greater Moses who gives the law from the mountain. It also teaches the church how to live as his disciples until he returns.
matthew.jesus: Messiah and King; teacher with authority; “God with us” (Immanuel, 1:23).
outline: Birth and childhood
Genealogy, the Magi, the flight to Egypt and Nazareth.
Preparation
Baptism, temptation, the call of the first disciples.
Sermon on the Mount
The first of five long teaching blocks, on life in God’s kingdom.
Ten miracles
Healings and power over storm and demons.
Sending out the Twelve
The second teaching block, on mission.
Welcome and opposition
John’s question, Sabbath conflicts, “something greater than Solomon”.
Parables of the kingdom
The third teaching block.
Who is Jesus?
Feeding the crowds, Peter’s confession (16), the Transfiguration (17).
Life in the community
The fourth teaching block, on greatness, sin and forgiveness.
Toward Jerusalem
Teaching on marriage, wealth and service.
Confrontation in Jerusalem
Entry, the Temple, debates and the woes on the scribes and Pharisees.
Teaching on the end
The fifth teaching block, on watching and being ready.
Arrest, trial and cross
Last Supper, Gethsemane, Pilate, crucifixion.
Resurrection and commission
The empty tomb and the Great Commission.
themes: Matthew’s favorite phrase. No other Gospel uses it; the others say “kingdom of God”.
Repeated lines such as “this took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet” tie events to Scripture.
Chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18 and 24–25 each end with a note that Jesus had finished speaking.
Only Matthew uses the word “church” (16:18; 18:17), and it gives rules for life together.
A righteousness that goes deeper than rule-keeping (5:20).
unique: The visit of the Magi and the flight to Egypt
The full Sermon on the Mount
Parables of the weeds, the hidden treasure, the pearl and the net
The unforgiving servant, the workers in the vineyard, the two sons, the ten bridesmaids and the sheep and goats
The coin in the fish’s mouth (17:24–27)
The guard at the tomb and the Great Commission
matthew.caution: Matthew shares much of its material with Mark and Luke. Most scholars think Matthew used Mark; this is the most widely held view, not a settled fact.

mark.name: Mark
mark.tag: Jesus the suffering Son of God, in action
facts: John Mark, a companion of Peter and Paul. Papias (quoted by Eusebius) says Mark wrote down Peter’s teaching accurately but not in order. The book itself does not name its author.
Most scholars say the late 60s to early 70s, near the Roman war in Judea. Some date it a little earlier.
Tradition says Rome. Others suggest Syria or Galilee.
Probably non-Jewish believers facing pressure. Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4) and translates Aramaic phrases such as “Talitha koum” (5:41).
An ancient biography. It is the shortest Gospel and moves quickly.
Opens with “the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1). The earliest manuscripts end at 16:8. Verses 9–20 appear in later copies.
mark.purpose: Mark shows who Jesus is through what he does, and it insists that the Messiah’s path is service and suffering. The centurion’s words at the cross, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39), are the book’s high point.
mark.jesus: The Son of God who serves, suffers and gives his life as a ransom (10:45).
outline: Prologue and first ministry
John the Baptist, baptism, temptation, call of the first disciples, first healings.
Early conflicts
Debates over forgiveness, fasting and the Sabbath; the Twelve are chosen.
Parables and power
The sower; calming the storm; the demoniac; Jairus’s daughter.
Crowds and bread
Rejection at Nazareth, John’s death, two feedings, Peter’s confession (8:29).
On the way to Jerusalem
Three predictions of suffering; teaching on greatness, marriage, riches; Bartimaeus.
Jerusalem
Entry, the Temple, controversies and the teaching on the end.
Passion
Anointing, Last Supper, Gethsemane, trial and crucifixion.
Empty tomb
The women at the tomb; the ending is debated.
themes: Mark’s favorite word for the pace of the story. The Greek word (euthys) is far more frequent in Mark than in Matthew or Luke, though English versions vary how they translate it.
Jesus often tells people not to tell who he is, until the cross reveals it.
The disciples often misunderstand. The section on the road to Jerusalem is about following Jesus in service.
Jesus’ chosen title: glorious, but also one who suffers (8:31; 10:45).
Fewer long speeches and more miracles per page than the other Gospels.
unique: The seed that grows by itself (4:26–29)
Healing of a deaf man with a speech impediment (7:31–37)
The two-stage healing of a blind man at Bethsaida (8:22–26)
The young man who fled naked at Gethsemane (14:51–52)
The Aramaic words of Jesus, such as “Ephphatha” (7:34) and “Abba” (14:36)
mark.caution: Mark 16:9–20 is missing from the oldest manuscripts, and some early copies have a different short ending. Most translations print it with a note.

luke.name: Luke
luke.tag: Jesus the Savior of all people, told as an orderly account
facts: Luke, a physician and companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14; 2 Timothy 4:11). He also wrote Acts, which says it continues “the first book” (Acts 1:1).
Scholars range from the 60s to the 80s AD. Many choose the 80s.
Theophilus (“lover of God”), a person of standing, and through him readers beyond the Jewish world.
Greek historical writing with a formal opening (1:1–4). It is the longest Gospel.
Opens with the preface to Theophilus (1:1–4). Ends with the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy and praising God in the temple (24:52–53).
luke.purpose: Luke writes so that Theophilus “may know the certainty of the things you have been taught” (1:4). It stresses that salvation is for everyone, especially the poor, the outcast and the lost.
luke.jesus: The Savior and Lord for all people; a prophet who is also the Son of God.
outline: Births and childhood
Announcements to Zechariah and Mary, the birth in Bethlehem, Jesus at twelve.
Preparation
John the Baptist, the genealogy, temptation, the sermon at Nazareth.
Ministry in Galilee
Call of disciples, the Sermon on the Plain (6), healings, Peter’s confession (9).
The journey to Jerusalem
Starts at 9:51. Many parables found only in Luke: the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, Zacchaeus.
Teaching in Jerusalem
Temple debates and the teaching on the end.
Arrest, trial and cross
Last Supper, Gethsemane, Pilate and Herod, crucifixion.
Resurrection and ascension
The road to Emmaus, the appearance to the disciples, the ascension.
themes: From Simeon’s “light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:32) to the final commission to all nations (24:47).
Shepherds, tax collectors, lepers, the widow, and the lost sheep, coin and son (ch. 15).
Jesus prays often at key moments, and the Spirit fills Jesus, Mary and Elizabeth.
Luke names more women than the other Gospels: Elizabeth, Mary, Anna, Joanna, Mary and Martha.
Table scenes and celebrations recur, from Levi’s feast to Emmaus.
unique: The announcements to Zechariah and Mary, and the songs (Magnificat, Benedictus)
The shepherds and the boy Jesus in the Temple
The Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son
Zacchaeus; the rich man and Lazarus; the persistent widow; the Pharisee and tax collector
“Father, forgive them” and the promise to the thief on the cross
luke.caution: Luke and Acts were meant to be read together. The Gospel’s last scene is the first scene of Acts.

john.name: John
john.tag: Jesus the eternal Word, who gives life to all who believe
facts: John son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. The Gospel names “the disciple whom Jesus loved” as its source and witness (21:20–24). Some scholars suggest another John or another follower.
Usually the 80s–90s AD. A small papyrus fragment (P52) of John 18 from the early-to-mid 2nd century shows it was in circulation soon after.
Believers and seekers, Jewish and Gentile. It states its aim openly in 20:30–31.
A theological biography built around signs and long conversations. Most of its stories are not found in the other three Gospels.
Opens with “In the beginning was the Word” (1:1). Ends with the note that the world itself could not hold all the books that would be written about what Jesus did (21:25).
john.purpose: “But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (20:31).
john.jesus: The eternal Word made flesh; the Son who reveals the Father and gives life.
outline: Prologue and first witnesses
The Word, John the Baptist, the first disciples.
First signs and conversations
Cana; the Temple; Nicodemus; the Samaritan woman; the official’s son.
Bethesda and the Bread of Life
The healing at the pool, the feeding of the five thousand and the Bread of Life.
Feasts and conflict
Tabernacles and Dedication; the man born blind; the Good Shepherd.
Lazarus and the turning point
The raising of Lazarus and the plot to kill Jesus; the entry into Jerusalem.
The Upper Room
Foot washing, the farewell teaching and Jesus’ prayer.
Arrest, trial and cross
Gethsemane, Annas and Pilate, crucifixion.
Resurrection
Mary Magdalene, the disciples, Thomas.
Epilogue
Breakfast on the shore; Peter restored.
themes: The verb “believe” appears far more in John than in any other Gospel (see the table below).
Miracles are called “signs”. Seven are usually counted: water to wine, the official’s son, the paralytic at Bethesda, the five thousand, walking on water, the man born blind, and Lazarus.

Seven sayings with a picture: bread of life (6:35), light of the world (8:12), the gate (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6), the true vine (15:1).
Light and darkness, truth and the world
Pairs of opposites run through the book.
Jesus speaks constantly of the Father who sent him.
unique: The man born blind (ch. 9) and the raising of Lazarus (ch. 11)
The foot washing and the farewell teaching (ch. 13–17)
Thomas (20:24–29) and the breakfast on the shore (ch. 21)
john.caution: John has little overlap with the other Gospels and orders events differently, for example placing the Temple cleansing early in Jesus’ ministry (2:13–22).

acts.name: Acts
acts.tag: The risen Jesus keeps working through the Holy Spirit as the church grows from Jerusalem to Rome
facts: Luke, the physician and Paul's traveling companion. The book does not name its author. It is the second volume of a two-part work that begins with the Gospel of Luke (compare Luke 1:1-4 and Acts 1:1).
Probably about AD 62-80. It ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome about AD 60-62, and some scholars date the writing soon after, others in the 80s.
Unknown. Rome, Antioch, and Greece have all been suggested.
Theophilus (1:1), a Greek name meaning “loved by God,” and through him a mixed Jewish and Gentile readership.
Historical narrative in Greek, with many speeches. Four sections use “we” (16:10-17; 20:5-15; 21:1-18; 27:1–28:16), which suggests the writer was there.
Opens with “In my first book, O Theophilus” (1:1). Ends with Paul preaching the kingdom of God “without hindrance” (28:31).
acts.purpose: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8). The book follows that outline: Jerusalem (1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), and then out through the Roman world to Rome (13–28).
acts.jesus: The risen and ascended Lord, who keeps acting and speaking through the Holy Spirit and through his people (1:1; 9:5; 26:15).
outline: The promise and the Spirit
The Ascension, Matthias chosen, and the Spirit comes at Pentecost.
The church in Jerusalem
Healing at the Temple, arrests, Ananias and Sapphira, and Gamaliel’s advice.
Seven chosen; Stephen
Service for the widows, and the first martyr’s speech.
Samaria and Damascus
Philip in Samaria, the Ethiopian official, and Saul meets Jesus.
The Gentiles and Antioch
Peter and Cornelius, the church at Antioch, and Peter freed from prison.
First journey
Barnabas and Saul on Cyprus and in Galatia.
The Jerusalem council
Gentiles are saved by grace without keeping the law of Moses.
Second journey
Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, and eighteen months in Corinth.
Third journey
Two years in Ephesus, Eutychus, and the farewell at Miletus.
Arrest in Jerusalem
The Temple riot, Paul’s defense, and the plot of the forty.
Trials in Caesarea
Before Felix, Festus, and King Agrippa.
The voyage to Rome
The storm, the shipwreck on Malta, and Paul in Rome.
themes: The Spirit is the main actor. He comes at Pentecost (2), falls on Samaritans (8) and Gentiles (10), and guides the missionaries (13:2; 16:6-10).
“Witness” is the book’s key word (1:8). The apostles and others tell what they have seen and heard.
It moves from Jews to Samaritans (8), an Ethiopian (8), a Roman centurion (10), and the cities of Greece and Asia.
The believers pray, share meals, and share goods (2:42-47; 4:32-35).
Stephen, James, Peter, and Paul are arrested, beaten, or killed, yet the word keeps spreading (12:24; 28:31).
unique: Cornelius and the first Gentile believers (ch. 10)
acts.caution: Luke is selective. He follows Peter and then Paul, and says little about the spread of the gospel to Egypt, Africa, and the East. The book ends before Paul’s trial, and its dates are estimates.

romans.name: Romans
romans.full: The Letter of Paul to the Romans
romans.tag: The gospel reveals God’s righteousness: all are sinners, all who believe are justified, and the Spirit makes them new
facts: Paul, who calls himself “a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle” (1:1). He dictated the letter to Tertius, who adds his own greeting in 16:22. Almost no scholar doubts that Paul wrote it.
About AD 57, near the end of Paul’s third journey, during the three months he spent in Greece (Acts 20:2-3).
Probably Corinth. Phoebe of nearby Cenchreae carries the letter (16:1-2), and Paul’s host Gaius (16:23; 1 Cor 1:14) lived in Corinth.
The believers in Rome. Paul had not founded or visited this church (1:10-13), which seems to have begun with Jewish believers and grown to include many Gentiles.
A letter, but unlike most of Paul’s, it is not answering a crisis. It lays out his gospel in order, often as a conversation with an imagined objector (2:1-5; 3:1-9; 9:19-21).
Opens with “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God” (1:1). Ends with “to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen” (16:27).
romans.purpose: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, and also to the Greek” (1:16). Paul wanted the Roman church to understand the gospel fully, to live as one body of Jews and Gentiles, and to support his planned mission to Spain (15:23-24).
romans.jesus: The one through whom God sets sinners right. Christ died for the ungodly (5:6-8), was raised for our justification (4:25), and is the second Adam who undoes the first Adam’s fall (5:12-21).
outline: Greeting and theme
Paul introduces himself, states the gospel, and says why he wants to visit Rome.
Everyone is guilty
Gentiles and Jews alike are under sin, and no one is made right by works of the law.
Made right by faith
God’s righteousness comes through Jesus and is received by faith, as Abraham shows. The result is peace with God.
New life in Christ and the Spirit
Believers died to sin, are freed from the law’s condemnation, and are led by the Spirit toward future glory.
Israel and God’s promises
Paul grieves over Israel, explains God’s choice, and expects Israel’s restoration.
Living out the gospel
Worship with the whole life, love, respect for authorities, and welcome for those who differ.
Greetings
Paul names dozens of friends, including many women, and warns against divisions.
themes: God is both just and the one who makes sinners right (3:21-26). It is a gift received by faith, not earned.
Jew and Gentile alike have fallen short (3:9, 23). Everyone needs the same rescue.
Abraham was counted right before God because he believed (4:3), and the same is true for all who believe in Jesus.
The Spirit frees, adopts, prays with believers, and guarantees future glory (ch. 8).
God has not abandoned Israel, and Gentiles are grafted in. Both are urged to welcome each other (11; 14-15).
unique: The case that all have sinned (1:18–3:20)
Dying and rising with Christ in baptism (ch. 6)
The olive tree and Israel’s future (ch. 11)
romans.caution: Some of Romans is hard and has been read in very different ways, especially chapter 7 (whose “I” is this?), chapter 9 (how does God’s choice relate to human response?), and 13:1-7 (how far does obedience to rulers go?). Faithful readers disagree on these, so it is worth reading slowly.

1-corinthians.name: 1 Corinthians
1-corinthians.full: The First Letter of Paul to the Corinthians
1-corinthians.tag: Paul answers a divided, gifted, struggling church about unity, morality, worship, and the resurrection
facts: Paul, with “our brother Sosthenes” (1:1). Paul wrote more than one letter to Corinth (5:9), and this is the first one that survives.
About AD 53-55, toward the end of Paul’s nearly three years in Ephesus (Acts 19; 1 Cor 16:8).
Ephesus. Paul plans to stay there until Pentecost (16:8). Messengers had come from Chloe’s household (1:11) and the church had written to him (7:1).
The church in Corinth, which Paul started on his second journey and stayed with for eighteen months (Acts 18:1-18). Most members were Gentiles, and few were wealthy or well born (1:26).
A pastoral letter that takes up problems one by one. Phrases like “now concerning” (7:1; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1) mark answers to the church’s questions.
Opens with “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1). Ends with “My love to all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen” (16:24).
1-corinthians.purpose: “I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree with one another and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in mind and thought” (1:10). Paul addresses divisions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, worship, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection.
1-corinthians.jesus: The crucified and risen Lord, who is the power and wisdom of God (1:24), the Passover lamb (5:7), the one to whom the Lord’s Supper points (11:23-26), and the “firstfruits” of the resurrection (15:20).
outline: Divisions and true wisdom
Paul rebukes factions and says the cross is God’s wisdom.
Immorality and lawsuits
A man living with his stepmother, believers suing each other, and the body as God’s temple.
Marriage and singleness
Paul answers questions about marriage, divorce, and staying as one is.
Food offered to idols
Knowledge, love, and freedom, with warnings from Israel’s wilderness years.
Worship and gifts
Head coverings, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts, the body, and love (ch. 13).
The resurrection
Christ has been raised, and so will believers.
The collection and greetings
The offering for Jerusalem, travel plans, and closing words.
themes: God’s wisdom looks like foolishness to the world, and the cross is its center (1:18-25).
The church is one body with many members, so factions, pride, and neglect of the poor are all wrong (12:12-26).
Believers are not their own. They were bought with a price, so they honor God with their bodies (6:19-20).
Love is the best way, and without it even great gifts count for nothing (ch. 13).
Christ’s resurrection is the foundation of the gospel and the promise of believers’ future bodies (ch. 15).
unique: Freedom and food offered to idols (chs. 8–10)
1-corinthians.caution: Some passages are hard to apply across cultures, including head coverings (11:2-16) and women’s speaking in church (14:34-35). Christians disagree about what they require now. Also, Paul is answering their letter, so we often hear only half the conversation.

2-corinthians.name: 2 Corinthians
2-corinthians.full: The Second Letter of Paul to the Corinthians
2-corinthians.tag: Paul defends his ministry, shows God’s power in weakness, and appeals for reconciliation and generosity
facts: Paul, with Timothy (1:1). Some scholars think chapters 10-13 were written separately, but all of them are Paul’s.
About AD 55-56, a year or so after 1 Corinthians, during Paul’s third journey.
Macedonia (2:13; 7:5; 9:2), probably after meeting Titus there with news from Corinth.
The Corinthian church, where rival teachers had questioned Paul’s authority and he had made a painful visit (2:1).
A personal letter in which Paul sets out his understanding of ministry, suffering, and generosity. Its tone shifts from relief (chs. 1-7) to practical appeal (chs. 8-9) to sharp defense (chs. 10-13).

Opens with “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1). Ends with a blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (13:14).
2-corinthians.purpose: “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God” (5:20). Paul wants to restore trust with the church, to explain how true ministry works through weakness, to finish the collection for Jerusalem, and to prepare for his third visit.
2-corinthians.jesus: The one in whom all of God’s promises are “Yes” (1:20), who became poor so that we might become rich (8:9), and whose power is made perfect in weakness (12:9).
outline: Paul’s ministry and reconciliation
Comfort in suffering, the new covenant, treasure in jars of clay, and reconciliation with God.
The collection
Paul urges generosity for the poor in Jerusalem, using the churches of Macedonia as an example.
Paul defends his apostleship
Against the “super-apostles,” Paul boasts only in weakness, tells of his visions and thorn, and warns of his coming visit.
themes: Paul’s thorn taught him that Christ’s power is made perfect in weakness (12:9-10).
God comforts us in trouble so that we can comfort others (1:3-7).
God reconciled the world to himself in Christ and gave his people the message of reconciliation (5:18-21).
The Macedonians gave out of poverty, and Christ became poor for us (8:1-9).
Paul contrasts his suffering ministry with rivals who boasted in credentials (11:5-23).
unique: The new covenant and the veil (ch. 3)
2-corinthians.caution: The letter is the hardest of Paul’s to reconstruct. We don’t know exactly what happened on his “painful visit” or in the “severe letter” (2:1-4), and scholars debate whether chapters 10-13 were written after the rest. The reader hears only one side of an argument.

galatians.name: Galatians
galatians.full: The Letter of Paul to the Galatians
galatians.tag: Paul defends the gospel of grace: we are made right by faith in Christ, not by keeping the law
facts: Paul. He names himself at the start and again in 5:2, and he says he is writing in large letters with his own hand (6:11).

Uncertain. If it was written to churches in south Galatia (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe) it could be as early as AD 48-49, before the Jerusalem council. If written to north Galatia, it would be in the mid-50s.
Unknown. Antioch in Syria or somewhere on Paul’s later journeys are the common proposals.
The Galatian churches, mostly Gentile believers who were being told they needed circumcision and the law to be fully part of God’s people.
A letter with an angry tone. Paul says he is astonished (1:6) and doesn’t give thanks as in his other letters. It is a defense of the gospel and of his apostleship.
Opens with “Paul, an apostle—sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father” (1:1). Ends with “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen” (6:18).
galatians.purpose: “It was for freedom that Christ set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be burdened again by a yoke of slavery” (5:1). Paul writes because rival teachers were persuading Gentile believers to add circumcision and the law to faith in Christ.
galatians.jesus: The one who “gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age” (1:4), who redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us on the cross (3:13), and who lives in believers (2:20).
outline: Paul’s gospel and his apostleship
Paul says he received the gospel from Christ, was accepted by the Jerusalem leaders, and confronted Peter at Antioch.
Faith, not law
Abraham, the promise, and the Spirit show that people are justified by faith. Believers are sons, not slaves.
Living by the Spirit
Freedom is for love. The fruit of the Spirit replaces the works of the flesh.
themes: No one is justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ (2:16).
Believers are free from the law as a way to earn favor, and from slavery to sin (5:1, 13).
The Galatians received the Spirit by hearing with faith, and they are to walk by the Spirit (3:2-5; 5:16-25).
There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for all are one in Christ Jesus (3:28).
Paul will not accept any other gospel, even from an angel (1:6-9).
unique: Paul’s conversion told in his own words (1:11-24)
The allegory of Hagar and Sarah (4:21-31)
galatians.caution: Scholars disagree about who the “Galatians” were and when the letter was written. That affects how Galatians 2 (the Jerusalem visit) is lined up with Acts 11 and 15. The allegory in 4:21-31 is also unusual and Paul himself calls it an allegory.

ephesians.name: Ephesians
ephesians.full: The Letter of Paul to the Ephesians
ephesians.tag: God’s plan in Christ to unite all things, and what it means for the church to live as one new people
facts: Paul names himself in 1:1 and 3:1 and calls himself a prisoner. Some scholars think a follower wrote in his name, but the church has long accepted Paul.
About AD 60-62, when Paul was under house arrest in Rome (Acts 28), if written there.
Probably Rome. Some suggest Caesarea or Ephesus. Tychicus carried the letter (6:21-22).
The believers in Ephesus and likely other churches in Asia, since some old manuscripts lack “in Ephesus.” Paul had spent about three years in Ephesus (Acts 19-20).
A letter of two halves: doctrine (chs. 1-3) and daily living (chs. 4-6). It resembles Colossians in wording.
Opens with “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1). Ends with “Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love” (6:24).
ephesians.purpose: “He made known to us the mystery of His will, according to His good pleasure that He purposed in Christ, to be put into effect when the times reach their fulfillment, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together under one head, even Christ” (1:9-10). Paul shows how Jews and Gentiles are made one in Christ and urges them to live worthy of that calling.
ephesians.jesus: The head of the church and of all things (1:22; 4:15), who made peace by breaking down the wall between Jew and Gentile (2:14-16) and loves the church like a bridegroom (5:25).
outline: Blessings in Christ
God chose us, redeemed us, and sealed us with the Spirit. Paul prays that we know the power at work in us.
From death to life, and one new people
Saved by grace through faith. Jews and Gentiles are made one.
The mystery and Paul’s prayer
Gentiles are fellow heirs. Paul prays that they know the love of Christ.
Unity and growth
Walk worthy, use gifts, put off the old self.
Light, family, and the armor of God
Marriage, children and parents, slaves and masters, and spiritual warfare.
themes: Jews and Gentiles are united into one new humanity (2:14-22).
“By grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (2:8).
Chosen before the foundation of the world, to the praise of his glory (1:4-14).
Paul turns from belief to behavior with “walk” as the key word (4:1; 5:2, 8, 15).
Believers stand against evil powers with God’s armor (6:10-20).
unique: The wall of hostility broken down (2:11-22)
ephesians.caution: Ephesians has many words found nowhere else in Paul, which is why some scholars doubt he wrote it. The verses on marriage and slavery (5:21–6:9) reflect the Roman household and are read in different ways today.

philippians.name: Philippians
philippians.full: The Letter of Paul to the Philippians
philippians.tag: A joyful letter from prison: Christ’s humility, pressing on toward the goal, and contentment in all things
facts: Paul, with Timothy (1:1). Its authenticity is almost never doubted.
About AD 60-62 if written from Rome. Ephesus (mid-50s) and Caesarea (late 50s) have also been proposed.
Paul is in chains (1:7, 13), probably in Rome, with “the praetorian guard” and “Caesar’s household” nearby (1:13; 4:22).
The church in Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia. Paul founded it on his second journey (Acts 16), and it supported him repeatedly (4:15-16).
A friendly letter of thanks for a gift brought by Epaphroditus (4:18), with encouragement, warnings, and a call to unity.
Opens with “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus” (1:1). Ends with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit” (4:23).
philippians.purpose: “Only conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ… standing firm in one spirit, with one mind, striving together for the faith of the gospel” (1:27). Paul thanks the Philippians, updates them on his situation, and urges unity and joy in Christ.
philippians.jesus: Though in the form of God, he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was obedient to death on a cross. God has exalted him so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (2:6-11).
outline: Paul’s situation and prayer
Thanks, prayer, and news from prison, where the gospel advances.
Humility and the example of Christ
The Christ hymn, Timothy, and Epaphroditus.
Knowing Christ above all
Paul gives up his credentials and presses on toward the goal.
Joy, peace, and thanks
Rejoice, do not be anxious, think on good things, and the secret of contentment.
themes: The words for joy and rejoice appear about sixteen times in four short chapters.
Have the same mind that was in Christ Jesus (2:5).
“I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call” (3:14).
The Philippians shared in Paul’s work through prayer and gifts (1:5; 4:15).
“I have learned to be content whatever the circumstances” (4:11).
unique: “I can do all things through him” (4:13)
philippians.caution: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (4:13) is often quoted about achievement, but Paul is talking about contentment in need and in plenty. Also, the identity of the opponents in chapter 3 is debated.

colossians.name: Colossians
colossians.full: The Letter of Paul to the Colossians
colossians.tag: Christ is supreme over all creation and enough for the church, against empty human philosophies
facts: Paul, with Timothy (1:1). Some scholars question this, but most accept Paul.
About AD 60-62, during Paul’s imprisonment, probably in Rome.
Paul is in chains (4:3, 10, 18). Tychicus and Onesimus carry the letter (4:7-9), along with Philemon.
The church in Colossae, which Paul had not visited (2:1). It was started by Epaphras (1:7; 4:12). Laodicea and Hierapolis were nearby.
A letter that answers a teaching that combined philosophy, ritual rules, visions, and angels. Paul answers by pointing to Christ.
Opens with “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother” (1:1). Ends with “Grace be with you” (4:18).
colossians.purpose: “See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ. For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (2:8-9). Paul presents Christ as supreme and sufficient.
colossians.jesus: The image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, in whom all things were created and hold together, the head of the church (1:15-20).
outline: Thanks, prayer, and the supremacy of Christ
Paul thanks God for their faith and presents the great hymn about Christ.
Warning against false teaching
Fullness is in Christ, not in rules, visions, or philosophy.
New life in Christ
Put off the old, put on the new, and live in every relationship as for the Lord.
themes: He is Creator, Reconciler, and Head of the church (1:15-20).
Believers are complete in him and do not need extra rituals or powers (2:9-10).
Put off the old self and put on the new, which is renewed in knowledge (3:9-10).
Whatever you do, do it as for the Lord (3:17, 23).
“Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27).
unique: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27)
colossians.caution: The “Colossian heresy” is hard to identify. Paul gives only hints (2:16-23), and scholars have proposed Jewish mysticism, local folk religion, or Greek philosophy. We should not read too much into a few lines.

1-thessalonians.name: 1 Thessalonians
1-thessalonians.full: The First Letter of Paul to the Thessalonians
1-thessalonians.tag: Paul encourages a young, persecuted church: keep living to please God, and hope in Christ’s return
facts: Paul, with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy (1:1). Rarely doubted.
About AD 50-51, probably the earliest of Paul’s surviving letters, and so one of the earliest New Testament writings.
Corinth. Timothy had just returned from Thessalonica with news (3:6; Acts 18:5).
New believers, mostly Gentile, in Thessalonica, a port city and capital of Macedonia. Paul had been driven out after only a few weeks (Acts 17:1-10).
A warm pastoral letter, giving thanks, defending his motives, and answering questions about those who had died and the Lord’s return.
Opens with “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Ends with “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you” (5:28).
1-thessalonians.purpose: “We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who have no hope” (4:13). Paul wants to encourage a persecuted church, urge holy living, and clear up confusion about the return of Christ.
1-thessalonians.jesus: The Lord who will come again from heaven, raise the dead, and rescue us from the coming wrath (1:10; 4:16).
outline: Thanks for their faith
Paul gives thanks for their work of faith, labor of love, and endurance of hope.
Paul’s ministry and concern
His gentle care among them, his anxiety, and Timothy’s good report.
Holy living and the dead in Christ
Live to please God, love one another, and take heart about those who have died.
The day of the Lord and final words
Be ready, encourage one another, and a series of short commands.
themes: Each chapter ends with a reference to Christ’s coming (1:10; 2:19; 3:13; 4:16; 5:23).
Believers grieve, but not like those without hope (4:13-18).
Paul compares himself to a nursing mother and a father (2:7-12).
Work of faith, labor of love, endurance of hope (1:3).
unique: The day of the Lord as a thief (5:1-11)
1-thessalonians.caution: Christians disagree about the order of events at Christ’s return, and passages like 4:13-18 are used in different ways. Paul’s main point here is comfort, not a timetable.

2-thessalonians.name: 2 Thessalonians
2-thessalonians.full: The Second Letter of Paul to the Thessalonians
2-thessalonians.tag: Stand firm under persecution and don’t be shaken by claims that the day of the Lord has already come
facts: Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy (1:1). Some scholars doubt Pauline authorship, but most accept it.
About AD 50-52, a few months after 1 Thessalonians.
Probably Corinth, while Silas and Timothy were with him.
The Thessalonian church, which was still being persecuted and was troubled by a report that the day of the Lord had already come.
A short pastoral letter that gives thanks, corrects a misunderstanding, and rebukes those not working.
Opens with “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians” (1:1). Ends with “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all” (3:18).
2-thessalonians.purpose: “Concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered to Him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed by any spirit, message, or letter supposedly from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has already come” (2:1-2).
2-thessalonians.jesus: The Lord Jesus who will be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, and who will destroy the lawless one by the breath of his mouth (1:7; 2:8).
outline: Encouragement in persecution
Thanks for their growth, a promise of justice, and a prayer.
The day of the Lord
It has not come yet. The rebellion and the man of lawlessness come first.
Pray and work
Paul asks for prayer and rebukes idleness.
themes: God will repay those who afflict and give relief to those who are afflicted (1:5-10).
Don’t be alarmed by claims about the day of the Lord (2:1-2).
Something holds back the lawless one for now (2:6-7).
Paul worked night and day. Those unwilling to work should not eat (3:6-12).
Stand firm and hold to the traditions you were taught (2:15).
2-thessalonians.caution: Chapter 2 is one of the most puzzling passages in Paul, especially who or what restrains the lawless one. Christians have proposed many answers. Paul’s point is that believers should not be panicked.

1-timothy.name: 1 Timothy
1-timothy.full: The First Letter of Paul to Timothy
1-timothy.tag: Paul instructs his younger coworker on guarding sound teaching, ordering church life, and godly leadership
facts: Paul, who calls Timothy “my true child in the faith” (1:2). Some scholars think the Pastoral Letters were written after Paul’s death, but the church has long held they are his.
About AD 62-65, after Paul’s release from the imprisonment in Acts 28, if Paul wrote it.
Unknown. Paul has gone to Macedonia (1:3) after leaving Timothy in Ephesus.
Timothy, a young leader from Lystra with a Greek father and Jewish mother (Acts 16:1-3), and through him the church at Ephesus.
A letter of instruction from a mentor to a younger leader, covering false teaching, worship, church leaders, widows, and wealth.
Opens with “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior” (1:1). Ends with “Grace be with you all” (6:21).
1-timothy.purpose: “I am writing you these things, hoping to come to you soon; but if I am delayed, I write so that you will know how people ought to conduct themselves in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (3:14-15).
1-timothy.jesus: The one mediator between God and mankind, who gave himself as a ransom for all (2:5-6), manifested in the flesh (3:16), and the only Sovereign, King of kings (6:15).
outline: Guard the teaching
Paul urges Timothy to confront false teachers and thanks God for his own mercy.
Order in the church
Prayer, men and women in worship, and qualifications for overseers and deacons.
False teaching and Timothy’s example
Liars forbid marriage and foods. Timothy should be an example.
Widows, elders, slaves, and money
Practical care within the church and a warning about the love of money.
themes: Paul warns against myths, endless genealogies, and false teaching (1:3-7; 4:1-5).
Overseers and deacons must be above reproach (ch. 3).
Prayer, for kings and all in authority, that all may be saved (2:1-4).
The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (6:10).
Train yourself for godliness, with contentment (4:7-8; 6:6).
1-timothy.caution: Passages on women’s roles (2:8-15) are among the most discussed in the New Testament, and Christians who respect Scripture read them differently. Context in Ephesus, where false teachers were targeting households, matters for understanding them.

2-timothy.name: 2 Timothy
2-timothy.full: The Second Letter of Paul to Timothy
2-timothy.tag: Paul’s last letter: a farewell charge to stay faithful, endure hardship, and hold to Scripture
facts: Paul, who calls Timothy “my beloved child” (1:2). Some scholars question the Pastoral Letters, but the church has long attributed them to Paul.
About AD 64-67, probably near the end of Paul’s life.
Rome, in prison and in chains (1:8, 16-17; 2:9). Unlike the earlier imprisonment, he expects to die (4:6-8).
Timothy, probably in Ephesus, whom Paul asks to come quickly before winter (4:9, 21).
A personal farewell letter combining warm memories, charges, and warnings.
Opens with “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1). Ends with “Grace be with you” (4:22).
2-timothy.purpose: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (4:7). Paul charges Timothy to carry on the gospel after him, enduring suffering, holding to sound teaching, and preaching the word.
2-timothy.jesus: Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, descended from David (2:8), who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (1:10).
outline: Do not be ashamed
Paul remembers Timothy’s faith and urges him to rekindle his gift.
Be strong and endure
Soldier, athlete, and farmer. Handle the word rightly and avoid quarrels.
Last days and Scripture
Difficult times, and the God-breathed Scriptures.
The final charge
“Preach the word.” Paul’s farewell, requests, and personal notes.
themes: Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus (2:3).
What you have heard from me, entrust to faithful men (2:2).
All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable (3:16-17).
Do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord or of me (1:8).
2-timothy.caution: “God-breathed” (3:16) refers first to the Old Testament Scriptures Timothy had known from childhood. How that applies to the whole Bible is a question Christians have long discussed.

titus.name: Titus
titus.full: The Letter of Paul to Titus
titus.tag: Appoint good leaders in Crete and teach everyone to live out the gospel in ordinary life
facts: Paul, “a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). Some scholars question the Pastoral Letters, but the church has long attributed them to Paul.
About AD 63-65, between Paul’s two Roman imprisonments, if Paul wrote it.
Unknown. Paul plans to spend the winter in Nicopolis (3:12).
Titus, a Gentile convert who had worked with Paul (Galatians 2:1-3; 2 Cor 8), now left on Crete to organize the churches.
A short letter of practical advice about leaders, different groups in the church, and the grace that trains believers.
Opens with “Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). Ends with “Grace be with you all” (3:15).
titus.purpose: “This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put in order what remained and appoint elders in every town as I directed you” (1:5). Paul wants Titus to set up good leaders, silence false teachers, and teach a life that adorns the gospel.
titus.jesus: Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem us and purify a people for his own possession (2:13-14).
outline: Appoint elders and silence false teachers
Qualifications for elders, and the problem of Cretan false teachers.
Teach sound doctrine in daily life
Instructions for older men and women, younger people, and slaves, grounded in grace.
Good works and avoiding quarrels
Submit to authorities, remember mercy, and avoid foolish controversies.
themes: The word “good” and “good works” appears again and again (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14).
The grace of God teaches us to renounce ungodliness (2:11-12).
The church must hold to the trustworthy word (1:9; 2:1).
Elders must be blameless and hold firm to the word (1:5-9).
“He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (3:5).
titus.caution: Paul quotes a Cretan poet’s harsh view of Cretans (1:12). It is a quotation from Epimenides, not Paul’s general view of an ethnic group. Notes about the end of Paul’s life are tradition, not scripture.

philemon.name: Philemon
philemon.full: The Letter of Paul to Philemon
philemon.tag: Paul asks a Christian slave owner to welcome back his runaway slave as a brother
facts: Paul, “a prisoner of Christ Jesus,” with Timothy (v.1). No serious doubt exists about authorship.
About AD 60-62, at the same time as Colossians.
Prison, probably in Rome. Onesimus was with Paul (v.10), and Tychicus took both Colossians and Philemon to Colossae.
Philemon, a slave owner and a believer in Colossae who had been converted through Paul (v.19), and the church in his home.
A short personal letter, a persuasive appeal, with careful wordplay.
Opens with “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother” (v.1). Ends with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit” (v.25).
philemon.purpose: “Perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother” (vv.15-16). Paul appeals for Philemon to forgive and welcome Onesimus.
philemon.jesus: The model of one who takes another’s debt on himself: “If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account” (v.18).
outline: The whole letter
Greeting and thanks (vv.1-7), the appeal for Onesimus (vv.8-21), and final requests and greetings (vv.22-25).
themes: Paul appeals for love, not command.
Onesimus is now a beloved brother, in the flesh and in the Lord (v.16).
Paul offers to pay what Onesimus owes (vv.18-19).
Paul could command, but appeals on the basis of love (vv.8-9).
Welcome him as you would welcome me (v.17).
unique: A play on the name Onesimus, meaning “useful” (vv.10-11)
philemon.caution: Paul does not directly call for slavery to end, and the letter has been used both to defend slavery and to oppose it. The letter’s own logic, that a slave is a brother, undermines the institution, though Paul does not say it outright.

hebrews.name: Hebrews
hebrews.tag: Jesus is greater than angels, Moses, the priests, and the sacrifices, so hold fast and keep going
facts: Unknown. The writer knew Timothy (13:23), wrote excellent Greek, and used the Greek Old Testament. Origen said “only God knows” who wrote it.
Probably before AD 70, since it speaks of priests still offering sacrifices (8:4; 10:1-2), though not decisively.
Unknown. “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24) could mean it was written from Italy or to Italy.
Jewish Christians who had endured persecution earlier (10:32-34) and were growing weary and tempted to abandon the faith or return to Judaism.
A “word of exhortation” (13:22): a sermon built from Scripture with alternating teaching and warnings.

Opens with “In the past God spoke to our fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son” (1:1-2). Ends with “Grace be with you all” (13:25).
hebrews.purpose: “Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to the faith we profess” (4:14). The writer shows that Jesus is the final and complete revelation and sacrifice, and calls readers to perseverance.
hebrews.jesus: The radiance of God’s glory, the exact imprint of his nature (1:3); a great high priest who offered himself once for all (7:27); the founder and perfecter of our faith (12:2).
outline: Jesus is greater than the angels
The Son, the exalted one, and the first warning.
Greater than Moses; the promised rest
Be faithful, and enter God’s rest.
A better priest
Jesus as a high priest in the order of Melchizedek.
A better covenant and sacrifice
The new covenant, the true tabernacle, and one sacrifice for sins.
The heroes of faith
A list from Abel to the prophets.
Endure and live in faith
Run the race, and practical exhortations.
themes: Better than the angels, Moses, Aaron’s priests, and the old sacrifices.
Warning passages urge readers not to drift or fall away (2:1-4; 6:4-6; 10:26-31; 12:25-29).
Faith is confidence in what we hope for (11:1).
Jesus sympathizes with our weakness and offers access to God (4:14-16).
hebrews.caution: The warning passages (especially 6:4-6 and 10:26-31) have been read in different ways, from warnings to genuine believers to descriptions of those who only appeared to believe. Melchizedek and the tabernacle imagery are also unfamiliar to many readers.

james.name: James
james.tag: Practical wisdom: real faith shows itself in works, in speech, in humility, and in patient endurance
facts: James, who calls himself “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Most scholars identify him as James the brother of Jesus (Galatians 1:19), the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15). He was martyred about AD 62.
Perhaps AD 45-50, if early, or about AD 60 if later.
Jewish believers living outside the land, “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” (1:1), many of them poor and mistreated by the rich (2:6; 5:1-6).
A letter rich with short commands and vivid images. It echoes Jesus’ teaching, especially the Sermon on the Mount, and the Old Testament wisdom books.

Opens with “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” (1:1). Ends with “whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death” (5:20).
james.purpose: “But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (1:22). James wants his readers to live out their faith: to endure trials, to care for the poor, to control the tongue, to be humble, and to be patient until the Lord comes.
james.jesus: “The Lord of glory” (2:1), the coming judge (5:7-9), and the one whose teaching James echoes throughout, especially the Sermon on the Mount.
outline: Trials and doing the word
Joy in trials, asking God for wisdom, and being doers, not just hearers.
Faith and works
Don’t favor the rich, and faith without works is dead.
The tongue and wisdom
Small things with great effect, and wisdom from above.
Worldliness and humility
Quarrels come from desires. Submit to God and draw near to him.
Riches, patience, and prayer
Judgment on the rich, patience like the farmer, and prayer for the sick.
themes: Count it all joy when you meet trials (1:2-4).
A small member that boasts great things (ch. 3).
Do not show favoritism, and the rich are warned (2:1-7; 5:1-6).
Pure, peaceable, gentle, and full of mercy (3:17).
james.caution: James and Paul seem to disagree about faith and works, but they use words differently. Paul argues against earning salvation by works of the law. James argues that faith that never acts is not real. The two agree that faith saves and that real faith produces fruit.

1-peter.name: 1 Peter
1-peter.tag: Hope and holiness for scattered believers who suffer for doing good
facts: Peter, “an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1), writing with the help of Silvanus (5:12). Some scholars question this, but the early church accepted it.
About AD 62-64, before or at the start of Nero’s persecution.
“Babylon” (5:13), almost certainly a code name for Rome.
Believers scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia (1:1), most of them Gentiles, who were facing insults and social pressure.
A pastoral letter that encourages believers to live as exiles and strangers, citing the Old Testament often.
Opens with “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion” (1:1). Ends with “Peace to all of you who are in Christ” (5:14).
1-peter.purpose: “I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it” (5:12). Peter encourages believers to stand firm, to live honorably among unbelievers, and to follow Christ’s example in suffering.
1-peter.jesus: The Lamb without blemish (1:19), the living cornerstone (2:4-8), the one who bore our sins on the tree (2:24), and the Chief Shepherd (5:4).
outline: A living hope and a call to holiness
Salvation, the prophets’ foretelling, and a call to be holy.
A chosen people and Christ’s example
Living stones, a royal priesthood, submission, and Christ who suffered.
Wives, husbands, and suffering for good
Doing good, giving a defense, and Christ’s triumph.
Suffering as a Christian
Arm yourselves with the same mind, and live for God.
Elders and humility
Shepherd the flock, humble yourselves, and resist the devil.
themes: Believers are foreigners in the world, with their true home elsewhere (1:1; 2:11).
Christ suffered and then entered glory, and the same pattern holds for his people (4:12-14).
We have been born again to a living hope through the resurrection (1:3).
A chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation (2:9).
Live such good lives among the Gentiles that they glorify God (2:12).
unique: Be ready to give a defense (3:15)
Do not be surprised by fiery trials (4:12-19)
1-peter.caution: 3:19-20 (Christ preaching to the spirits in prison) is among the hardest passages in the New Testament, with several different interpretations. Instructions to slaves, wives, and husbands (2:18–3:7) reflect Roman household life and are read in different ways today.

2-peter.name: 2 Peter
2-peter.tag: Grow in the knowledge of Christ, beware of false teachers, and wait for the Lord’s promised return
facts: “Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). Some scholars doubt Peter wrote it because of its style and its relationship to Jude, but the early church accepted it, if slowly.
About AD 64-68, shortly before Peter’s death (1:14).
Christian communities Peter has addressed before (3:1), now threatened by false teachers who scoff at the promise of Christ’s return.
A farewell letter (a “testament”) that reminds, warns, and encourages.
Opens with “Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). Ends with “To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen” (3:18).
2-peter.purpose: “I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder” (1:13). Peter wants his readers to grow in godliness, resist false teachers who deny Christ’s return, and remember the apostolic testimony.
2-peter.jesus: The Lord and Savior who shared his glory on the mountain (1:16-18), who will return like a thief (3:10), and in whom believers are to grow in grace and knowledge (3:18).
outline: Growing in Christ and the apostolic witness
Add virtue to faith, and remember Peter’s eyewitness account of the transfiguration.
False teachers
Their destructive heresies, greed, and judgment, with examples from the Old Testament.
The day of the Lord
Scoffers deny it, but the Lord is patient, and the day will come.
themes: Make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue (1:5-7).
“We did not follow cleverly devised myths” (1:16).
They will secretly bring in destructive heresies (2:1).
The Lord is not slow, but patient, not wishing that any should perish (3:9).
The heavens will pass away, and there will be new heavens and a new earth (3:10-13).
2-peter.caution: Many scholars question whether Peter wrote 2 Peter, and the early church was slow to accept it. Its close parallels with Jude are explained in different ways. Peter’s mention of Paul’s letters (3:15-16) shows these letters were already treated as Scripture.

1-john.name: 1 John
1-john.tag: Walk in the light, love one another, and know that you have eternal life in the Son of God
facts: The letter does not name its author. Early church writers from Irenaeus on give it to John the apostle, who is also credited with the Gospel of John and whose style the letter closely shares. Some scholars think an elder in John’s circle wrote it.
Usually dated about AD 85-100, and usually after the Gospel of John.
The letter does not say. Church tradition points to Ephesus and the churches of Roman Asia.
Churches that had been divided by teachers who left (2:19) and denied that Jesus had really come in the flesh (4:2-3).
A letter without an introduction or farewell, built around three tests of true faith: believe in Jesus, obey God, love one another.
Opens with “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes” (1:1). Ends with “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (5:21).
1-john.purpose: “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). John wants his readers to have assurance, to reject false teaching, and to love one another.
1-john.jesus: The Word of life (1:1), our advocate with the Father and atoning sacrifice for our sins (2:1-2), and the Son of God who came in the flesh (4:2).
outline: Walking in the light
Fellowship with God, confession of sin, obedience, and warning against the world.
Children of God
Loving one another and having confidence before God.
Testing the spirits and God’s love
God is love; we love because he first loved us.
Faith and eternal life
Believing in Jesus overcomes the world, and we can know we have life.
themes: God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1:5).
God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God (4:16).
These things are written that you may know you have eternal life (5:13).
Confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (4:2).
Whoever keeps his commandments abides in him (3:24).
1-john.caution: 1 John has strong contrasts (light and dark, love and hate, truth and lie). It speaks about sin in ways that seem to say believers cannot sin (3:6, 9), yet also admits that they do (1:8-10). Careful reading shows that John is speaking of continuing in sin as a habit.

2-john.name: 2 John
2-john.tag: Walk in truth and love, and do not welcome those who deny that Jesus came in the flesh
facts: The writer calls himself only “the elder” (v.1), as 3 John does. Early church writers from Irenaeus on give the letter to John the apostle. Some scholars think an elder named John in the apostle’s circle wrote it.
Usually dated about AD 85-100, near 1 John.
The letter does not say. Church tradition points to Ephesus, and a sister church sends greetings (v.13).
“The chosen lady and her children” (v.1), most often read as a church and its members, who received traveling teachers.
A short letter, roughly 245 Greek words, that would fit on one sheet of papyrus.
Opens with “The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth” (v.1). Ends with “The children of your elect sister send you greetings” (v.13).
2-john.purpose: “Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded” (v.8). The elder urges his readers to love one another, to remain in the teaching of Christ, and to be careful about whom they receive.
2-john.jesus: “Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father” (v.3), whose coming “in the flesh” (v.7) the deceivers refuse to confess.
outline: The whole letter
Greeting and truth (vv.1-3), love and commandment (vv.4-6), deceivers and warning (vv.7-11), and farewell (vv.12-13).
themes: Walking in truth and loving one another go together (vv.4-6).
Whoever abides in it has both the Father and the Son (v.9).
Many deceivers have gone out who deny the incarnation (v.7).
Do not welcome those who bring a false teaching (vv.10-11).
2-john.caution: The instruction not to welcome a false teacher (vv.10-11) is addressed to a specific situation of traveling teachers who relied on hospitality, and should not be read as permission to shun people who disagree on lesser matters.

3-john.name: 3 John
3-john.tag: Support the traveling teachers of the truth, and do not follow a church leader who refuses them
facts: The writer calls himself only “the elder” (v.1), as 2 John does. Church tradition gives the letter to John the apostle. Some scholars think an elder named John in the apostle’s circle wrote it.
Usually dated about AD 85-100, near 1 and 2 John.
The letter does not say. Church tradition points to Ephesus.
Gaius (v.1), a friend of the elder who took traveling brothers into his home. His town is not named.
A short personal letter. At about 219 Greek words it is the shortest book in the New Testament.
Opens with “The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth” (v.1). Ends with “Greet each of our friends there by name” (v.14).
3-john.purpose: “Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you” (v.5). The elder praises Gaius for his hospitality, warns about Diotrephes, and speaks well of Demetrius.
3-john.jesus: The letter never uses the words Jesus or Christ. The brothers went out “on behalf of the Name” (v.7), and the elder’s joy is to hear that his children are walking in the truth (v.4).
outline: The whole letter
Commendation of Gaius (vv.1-8), the problem of Diotrephes (vv.9-10), a good example in Demetrius (vv.11-12), and closing (vv.13-14).
themes: Support those who went out on behalf of the Name (vv.5-8).
No greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth (v.4).
Do not imitate what is evil, but what is good (v.11).
unique: Diotrephes who loves to be first (v.9)
3-john.caution: Verse 2 follows the usual health wish of a Greek letter and is one friend’s prayer for another. It is not a promise of wealth. The letter gives only the elder’s side of the trouble with Diotrephes, and his actions can be read in more than one way.

jude.name: Jude
jude.tag: Contend for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints, and keep yourselves in the love of God
facts: Jude (Judas), “a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (v.1). Most readers take him to be one of the brothers of Jesus (Mark 6:3). Some scholars think the letter was written later in his name.
Uncertain: about AD 50-90. If 2 Peter used Jude, Jude is the earlier of the two.
The letter does not say. The land of Israel or Syria is often suggested.
Believers among whom “certain men have crept in” (v.4), turning grace into a license for immorality.
A short, urgent letter of 25 verses, full of Old Testament examples and vivid pictures. Verses 4-18 run alongside 2 Peter 2.

Opens with “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (v.1). Ends with a doxology: “to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord” (v.25).
jude.purpose: “I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (v.3). Jude warns about people who twist grace, reminds his readers what the apostles foretold, and tells them to keep themselves in God’s love and to show mercy.
jude.jesus: “Our only Master and Lord” (v.4), in whom believers are kept (v.1), whose mercy brings eternal life (v.21), and through whom glory is given to God (v.25).
outline: The whole letter
Greeting (vv.1-2), the occasion (vv.3-4), examples of judgment (vv.5-16), exhortations to remember and persevere (vv.17-23), and a doxology (vv.24-25).
themes: The faith was “entrusted once for all to the saints” (v.3).
Examples from Israel, the angels and Sodom (vv.5-7).
Keep yourselves in the love of God (v.21).
Have mercy on those who doubt (v.22).
He is able to keep you from stumbling (v.24).
unique: The angels who abandoned their proper dwelling (v.6)
jude.caution: Jude quotes the Book of Enoch (vv.14-15) and uses a Jewish story about Michael and the body of Moses (v.9). Neither is in the Old Testament, and Christians have explained Jude’s use of them in different ways. In verse 5 the old copies differ between “Jesus” and “the Lord.”

revelation.name: Revelation
revelation.tag: The risen Christ reveals to John that God’s purposes will triumph: evil will fall, and God will dwell with his people forever
facts: John, who says he was on Patmos “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9). Early Christian writers identified him as the apostle John, though some ancient and modern readers suggest another John.
Most scholars date it to the reign of Domitian, about AD 95. A minority suggest the late 60s, after Nero.
Patmos, a small island in the Aegean Sea off the coast of Asia, where John was in exile.
Seven churches in Asia (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea), facing pressure to worship the emperor and compromise with the surrounding culture.
A mix of three types: a prophecy (1:3), a letter (1:4; chapters 2-3), and an apocalypse, a style of vision-writing full of symbols, numbers, and images drawn from the Old Testament.

Opens with “This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass” (1:1). Ends with “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen” (22:21).
revelation.purpose: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near” (1:3). Revelation unveils Jesus Christ as Lord of history, encourages believers to be faithful under pressure, and shows God’s final victory over evil.
revelation.jesus: The faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead (1:5), the Alpha and the Omega (22:13), the Lion of the tribe of Judah who is also the slain Lamb (5:5-6), the Word of God and King of kings (19:11-16).
outline: The vision of Christ
John on Patmos sees the risen Christ among the lampstands.
Letters to seven churches
Christ’s words of praise, warning, and promise to each church.
The throne and the Lamb
Worship in heaven, and the scroll opened by the Lamb.
Seals and trumpets
Judgments unfold, the 144,000, the two witnesses, and the seventh trumpet.
The dragon, the beasts, and the Lamb
Conflict between the woman, the dragon, the beasts, and the Lamb with his people.
The bowls of wrath
Seven bowls poured out, ending at Armageddon.
The fall of Babylon and the return of Christ
The great prostitute falls, the wedding feast of the Lamb, and the rider on a white horse.
The thousand years and the final judgment
Satan bound, the reign of the saints, the final defeat of evil, and the great white throne.
New heaven and new earth
The holy city comes down, God dwells with his people, and the river of life.
themes: Jesus is the ruler of the kings of the earth (1:5), the center of every vision.
Believers overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony (12:11).
Evil systems fall, and God’s justice is vindicated (6:10; 19:1-2).
Heaven’s scenes center on God and the Lamb (chs. 4–5; 7; 15; 19).
God makes all things new, and dwells with his people (21:1-5).
unique: The letters to the seven churches (chs. 2–3)
The throne room and the Lamb (chs. 4–5)
revelation.caution: Christians have read Revelation in very different ways: as events in John’s own day, as a sweep of church history, as events at the end of time, or as symbolic pictures of the struggle between good and evil in every age. Many details, such as the identity of the beast or the meaning of the thousand years, are debated. Those who study carefully disagree, so it is wise to read with humility.
